podcast.body: Produced by Nile Rodgers, this album helped David Bowie become a chart-topper again during the second British invasion, reaching number one on the US charts. The success of this album made Bowie a "chart-topper all over again." "New Wave 4 father David Bowie a chart-topper all over again, as his Nile Rogers produced Let's Dance reached number one."

podcast.body: Produced by Nile Rodgers, this album marked David Bowie's biggest commercial success and skillfully straddled the lines between alternative, post disco, and alt dance music. Its release in 1983 demonstrated how mainstream artists could embrace the new dance momentum. "And Let's Dance was the biggest album of his career."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Produced by Nile Rogers and Bowie's first under a new contract with the EMI label, this album was his determined bid to become a global pop star again by re-embracing a glossier, R&B-based rock sound. It peaked at number 4 on the Billboard album chart, his highest charting LP since 1976's "Station to Station," and was his first to go platinum in America, ushering in a new mid-80s "imperial phase." "That 1983 album, produced by Rogers, and Bowie's first in a new contract with the EMI label, was his bid to be a global pop star again."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.body: Recorded in just 17 days with a new session band, this album was a massive commercial success, selling over 6 million copies and becoming Bowie's best-selling album ever. The album, a hybrid of rock, dance, and funk, was groundbreaking for 1983 and led to the "Serious Moonlight Tour" which drew 2.6 million people across 16 countries. "Let's Dance was a massive success for Bowie, and drew 2.6 million people to the serious moonlight tour as it wound its way through 16 countries."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This album marked a strong start for David Bowie in the 1980s, showcasing his continued ability to evolve his sound and achieve commercial success. "The 80s started strong with the Let's Dance album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Peaked Too Soon - Bands That Were Ahead of Their Time

podcast.body: This album was conceived as a more commercially sounding record after Bowie's $17.5 million deal with EMI Records. Recorded with a new band of session players in just 17 days, including mixing, it was a massive and unexpected success, selling over six million copies and becoming Bowie's best-selling album of all time. Its hybrid rock dance funk sound was considered innovative for 1983. The album's success, however, caused Bowie to feel disconnected from his audience during the subsequent Serious Moonlight Tour. "Let's Dance was a massive success for Bowie and drew 2.6 million people to the serious Moonlight Tour as it wound through 16 countries."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This album, released the year before 1984, kicked off a hot streak for David Bowie. He continued this success into 1984 with singles like "Blue Jean," maintaining his strong presence in pop music. "David Bowie, who had just turned 37, kept up his hot streak that he'd kicked off the year before on the Let's Dance LP."
